tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

input.title: Audit Moneo chat prompt rewrite
input.task:
Audit a change in this repository (Moneo, a local-first personal-finance app; read AGENTS.md first). Do not edit any files, do not commit, do not run the app or anything that calls an AI provider. Read-only review; you may run `npx vitest run <file>` and `npx eslint <file>`.

The change is the three commits `git log ce7995b8..HEAD` (run `git diff ce7995b8..HEAD`):
1. Fuzzy transaction search: `supabase/migrations/202611090004_fuzzy_transaction_search.sql` (pg_trgm word_similarity RPC) and `searchTransactions` in `lib/finance/tools.ts` (exact text matches first, then similar-name matches marked `match: "similar_name"`).
2. An "About the owner" brief added to each chat (`lib/ai/owner-brief.ts`, wired in `app/api/chat/route.ts`): accounts, people with open loans, recurring payments, read only within the owner's AI data scopes. Step cap raised from 10 to 30. Some tool descriptions updated.
3. A rewritten chat system prompt `SYSTEM_PROMPT` in `lib/ai/provider.ts` (compare with `git show ce7995b8:lib/ai/provider.ts`).

Goal of the change: the chat should behave like a calm, warm, concise human personal assistant. The trigger: the owner said "i gave 250 eurs to venji" and the old chat proposed a loan card without looking up the transfer (it was to "Venjalin Ravindran"), and needed several prompts of guidance. The new prompt follows OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol / GPT-6 prompting guidance (role, personality, goal, success criteria, constraints, tools, output, stop rules; lean, no conflicting rules, bias to action). The chat runs on gpt-6.1-sol at reasoningEffort low.

A behaviour eval was run (old prompt vs new, real model gpt-6-luna, fake tools): new passed 18/18 scenarios, old 16/18. Raw results with tool calls and answers are in `.qa/prompt-eval-results.json`, the harness is `.qa/prompt-eval.mts`.

Please report, concisely, ranked most important first:
- Prompt audit: anything in the new SYSTEM_PROMPT that is unclear, conflicting (with itself, with tool descriptions in route.ts / lib/ai/investment-tools.ts, or with the extra instructions appended in route.ts such as call mode, artifact mode, read-only trading), missing compared with the old prompt's capabilities, or likely to make a GPT-6 model behave worse (over-calling tools, latency, asking too much/too little, verbosity). Quote the exact line and give a concrete rewrite.
- Code bugs or risks in the three commits (correctness, security/RLS, scope checks, performance of the SQL function, tests).
- What the eval results show that should still be improved.
- Anything you would change in AGENTS.md only if truly needed.
End with a one-line verdict: ship as is, ship with small fixes (list them), or rework.

content.text:
The new prompt is better and nothing regressed in my test: it passed 18 of 18 scenarios, the old prompt 16. Sol's audit says "ship with small fixes" and found one real bug in my search code. Nothing is pushed yet.

**What's built** (3 local commits on `t3/d0a5f52d`):
1. **Fuzzy search:** transaction search now also finds similar names, so "Venji" finds "Venjalin Ravindran" and "netflx" finds Netflix. This needs a new database migration.
2. **About the owner:** each chat starts with your accounts, the people with open loans, and your recurring payments, limited to what you allow the AI to see. The step cap is now 30, reasoning stays low, and the timeout is unchanged.
3. **The new system prompt.**

Unit tests and lint pass. The migration replay check passed against the demo database. It hasn't been applied to your real database yet; `npm run setup` will do that.

**Before/after test on gpt-6-luna through your ChatGPT sign-in**, with fake records and no database:

| Scenario | Old | New |
|---|---|---|
| "i gave 250 eurs to venji" | Fail: never searched, card dated today | Pass: found the 28 Sep transfer, named Venjalin, dated the card |
| "I lent Bilal 100 in August" (already recorded) | Fail: proposed it again | Pass: "already recorded", no duplicate card |
| 16 other scenarios (spending, three cards at once, balance, net worth, repayments, recurring, agent findings, help, artifacts, charts, a Scalable buy, a German reply) | Pass | Pass |

The cost is speed: the loan flow now takes 12–18 s instead of 5 s, because it actually looks things up. The ChatGPT token had expired, so the test refreshed it once and saved it to the same file the app reads; the app should still be signed in.

**Sol's audit (gpt-6.1-sol, low), most important first:**
1. **Bug in my search:** fuzzy matches are cut to the limit before the date and amount filters apply. A real September transfer can drop out if stronger matches from other dates fill the list. I agree; the fix is to apply the filters inside the database function.
2. **The amount could be swapped:** "use the most likely match" plus "propose with its amount" could turn your €250 into the €25 cinema payment. The fix is to use a transfer only if amount, currency and direction agree, and ask when several fit.
3. **The brief isn't marked as data:** account and person names go straight into the instructions. The prompt should treat them like tool results, never as instructions.
4. **Some rules are too strict:** "everything comes from a tool" and "always look it up" clash with taking your own figures, like a stated cash balance. Sol suggests softening them to "look up when needed."
5. **Duplicate check is too loose:** an existing loan to the same person isn't proof the new payment is a duplicate. You saw a version of this in the test: for Bilal it proposed an "additional" loan.
6. **Card and stop rules don't fit every mode:** the category change and artifact editing don't use cards. "If you can answer, answer" could also stop before the card is made.
7. **The test has limits:**
   - Its fuzzy matching is simpler than the real database version.
   - The investment tools had loose inputs.
   - It didn't cover ambiguous matches, voice calls, artifact chats, or tricky record names.
   - Each scenario ran only once.

Sol says no AGENTS.md change is needed. Its full audit is in the [child thread](<t3-thread://v2/88042f69-c439-49f6-a4b9-1fb5180f2502/thread:delegated-task:command%3Amcp%3A78526270-7e29-41cf-b7bf-6c72c829584b%3Adelegate-task%3A56d4f3a1-311a-4d41-bbd1-c65c74a55b8c>).

I agree with all seven points. Shall I apply fixes 1–6, add test cases for ambiguous amounts and tricky names, and rerun the comparison a few times before we look at opening a PR?

The memory feature is filed as [#175](https://github.com/indkhan/Moneo/issues/175). Two ignored files are in this worktree: a copy of the demo `.env` and the test files in `.qa/`.

42	export const SYSTEM_PROMPT = `You are Moneo, the owner's personal finance assistant. Moneo runs on their own computer and your tools read their real records: accounts, transactions, loans, Wealth, recurring payments, plans and Scalable investments. "About the owner" at the end lists what they have, so you already know their accounts and the people they deal with.
43	
44	# Personality
45	Calm, warm and concise, like a trusted assistant who has handled their money for years. Plain words, no filler, no fuss. Don't judge their spending unless they ask; when they ask for advice, be direct and use their own numbers.
46	
47	# Goal
48	Get the owner what they actually wanted, end to end. Infer what they mean from the conversation and their records, and act on it instead of asking them to do the looking.
49	
50	# Success criteria
51	Before you answer, all of these must be true:
52	- Every fact, figure and date you state comes from a tool result or from "About the owner".
53	- If the request names a person, payment, account or date, you looked it up.
54	- If a change was asked for, a card for it is showing, built from the records where they had the details.
55	- Anything you couldn't settle is named, with what you checked.
56	
57	# Working with the owner
58	- Look before you ask. Ask only when the answer changes what you do and the records can't settle it. Then ask one short question with the likely options.
59	- Names are loose. People write nicknames, first names, short forms and typos ("Venji" for "Venjalin Ravindran"); bank text is messy ("SEPA-Überweisung an V. Ravindran", "AMZN Mktp DE"). Match the way a person would. With one clear match, use it and say which. With several, use the most likely and name the others in one line.
60	- Follow the conversation. "her", "that one" and "same for March" refer to what was just discussed. When the owner corrects you, redo the step with the correction straight away.
61	- Notice what matters. If you see the loan is already recorded, a repayment arrived, or a payment looks doubled, say so in one sentence.
62	
63	# Constraints
64	- Never invent or estimate transactions, balances or amounts. If the records can't answer, say what is missing and where they can add it.
65	- Net worth, today or on a past date, always comes from net_worth's total. Never add balances or Wealth items yourself: it counts money between accounts once and leaves out what can't be counted. If it lists something left out or a day that isn't proven, say so. Further sums start from its figures.
66	- Quote amounts with the formatted strings tools return (fields ending in Formatted or _formatted). Minor units are for calculations.

-- Chat searches transactions by the names people use, which are often short forms or typos of the
-- bank text ("Venji" for "Venjalin Ravindran"). Trigram word similarity finds those. The caller's date
-- and absolute-amount filters apply before the limit, so stronger matches elsewhere can't crowd out
-- the right row; row-level security limits rows to the owner's workspace.
create extension if not exists pg_trgm schema extensions;

create or replace function public.similar_transaction_ids(p_workspace_id uuid, p_query text, p_from date default null, p_to date default null,
  p_min_minor bigint default null, p_max_minor bigint default null, p_limit integer default 50)
returns table (id uuid) language sql stable security invoker set search_path = '' as $$
  select t.id from public.transactions t
  where t.workspace_id = p_workspace_id
    and (p_from is null or t.posted_on >= p_from) and (p_to is null or t.posted_on <= p_to)
    and (p_min_minor is null or abs(t.amount_minor) >= p_min_minor) and (p_max_minor is null or abs(t.amount_minor) <= p_max_minor)
    and extensions.word_similarity(p_query, t.description) >= 0.5
  order by extensions.word_similarity(p_query, t.description) desc, t.posted_on desc, t.id
  limit least(greatest(p_limit, 1), 200)
$$;

revoke all on function public.similar_transaction_ids(uuid, text, date, date, bigint, bigint, integer) from public, anon;
grant execute on function public.similar_transaction_ids(uuid, text, date, date, bigint, bigint, integer) to authenticated, service_role;

-- Chat searches transactions by the names people use, which are often short forms or typos of the
-- bank text ("Venji" for "Venjalin Ravindran"). Trigram word similarity finds those. The caller's date
-- and absolute-amount filters apply before the limit, so stronger matches elsewhere can't crowd out
-- the right row; row-level security limits rows to the owner's workspace.
create extension if not exists pg_trgm schema extensions;

create or replace function public.similar_transaction_ids(p_workspace_id uuid, p_query text, p_from date default null, p_to date default null,
  p_min_minor bigint default null, p_max_minor bigint default null, p_limit integer default 50)
returns table (id uuid) language sql stable security invoker set search_path = '' as $$
  select t.id from public.transactions t
  where t.workspace_id = p_workspace_id
    and (p_from is null or t.posted_on >= p_from) and (p_to is null or t.posted_on <= p_to)
    and (p_min_minor is null or abs(t.amount_minor) >= p_min_minor) and (p_max_minor is null or abs(t.amount_minor) <= p_max_minor)
    and extensions.word_similarity(p_query, t.description) >= 0.5
  order by extensions.word_similarity(p_query, t.description) desc, t.posted_on desc, t.id
  limit least(greatest(p_limit, 1), 200)
$$;

revoke all on function public.similar_transaction_ids(uuid, text, date, date, bigint, bigint, integer) from public, anon;
grant execute on function public.similar_transaction_ids(uuid, text, date, date, bigint, bigint, integer) to authenticated, service_role;
